message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a Python program by BLACK-BOX probing. Never read Python library source; only run the binary.

The program is:
  instance = json.loads(args.a); schema = json.loads(args.b)
  validator = Draft7Validator(schema)
  errors = list(validator.iter_errors(instance)); tree = ErrorTree(errors)
  total = tree.total_errors
  first_pass = list(validator.iter_errors(instance)); second_pass = list(...)
  check1..3 = validator.is_valid(instance)
  schema_check1/2 = validator.check_schema(schema)
  tree1 = ErrorTree(first_pass); tree2 = ErrorTree(second_pass)
  print(total); print(len(first_pass)); print(len(second_pass)); print(check1..3); print(schema_check1/2); print(tree1.total_errors); print(tree2.total_errors)

So stdout is 10 lines: [treeTotal, nErrors, nErrors, bool, bool, bool, None, None, treeTotal, treeTotal].
Line 2 = the RAW COUNT of errors from iter_errors. Line 1 = ErrorTree total, which groups errors by (absolute instance path, validator keyword) in a dict, so two errors sharing both path and keyword COLLAPSE into one. The difference between line 1 and line 2 is the single most valuable signal you can extract — hunt for cases where they differ.
IMPORTANT: every print happens at the end, so ANY exception => EMPTY stdout and non-zero exit. Record exit codes.

Run it like this (ALWAYS redirect stderr away or capture separately; a harmless DeprecationWarning is always on stderr):
  /workspace/dataset/test18_executable --a '<instance json>' --b '<schema json>' 2>/dev/null; echo "EXIT=$?"

Use single-quoted shell args. Batch many cases into one bash call with a loop or a heredoc-driven script to be efficient; aim for 40+ distinct probe cases. When a case crashes, re-run it with 2>&1 to capture the Python exception type/message (that tells you WHICH operation failed and in what order).

I am reimplementing this in pure JavaScript. Report findings as precise, mechanical RULES that a reimplementer can encode, not prose impressions. Include the exact probe inputs and the exact 10-line stdout (or EMPTY + exit code) as evidence.


FAMILY: enum and const equality semantics (Python == with a boolean-vs-number guard).
Probe: enum [1] with instance true and with 1.0; enum [true] with 1; enum [0] with false; const 1 vs true; const true vs 1; const 1 vs 1.0; nested: const [1] with instance [true]; const {"a":1} with {"a":true}; enum [[1]] with [true]; enum with objects/arrays deep equality; enum [] (does check_schema reject an empty enum?); enum with duplicate entries (rejected by check_schema?); const null vs missing; string vs number "1" vs 1. Also very large ints for exact comparison (10000000000000000001 vs 10000000000000000002 — do they compare unequal, proving arbitrary precision?), and 1e19 vs 10000000000000000000.

input.family: enum and const equality semantics (Python `==` with a boolean-vs-number guard), Draft7Validator + ErrorTree

rules.rule: Output shape is invariant: exactly 10 lines = [treeTotal, n, n, B, B, B, "None", "None", treeTotal, treeTotal] where B is Python-style "True"/"False" (capitalized) and equals (n===0). Lines 2 and 3 are always identical (iter_errors is re-runnable, no generator exhaustion). Lines 1, 9, 10 are always identical. Lines 7,8 are the literal string "None" (check_schema returns None). Exit 0.
rules.evidence: --a '1' --b '{"allOf":[{"enum":[2]},{"enum":[3]}]}' -> `1 2 2 False False False None None 1 1` exit=0. Every non-crashing probe (100+) matched this shape.

rules.rule: Equality function `equal(a,b)` used by BOTH const and enum, applied recursively: (1) if a and b are the SAME OBJECT -> equal; (2) else if either is a string -> plain string equality (a string is never equal to an array/object even with the same elements); (3) else if both are arrays -> equal lengths AND element-wise equal(); (4) else if both are objects -> same key set AND value-wise equal(); (5) else compare unbool(a) == unbool(b), where unbool maps true/false to unique sentinels so a boolean is NEVER equal to any number.
Boolean/number guard is RECURSIVE, not just top-level. true !== 1, false !== 0 at any nesting depth, in both directions, for both enum and const.
rules.evidence: true|{"enum":[1]}->1 err; 1|{"enum":[true]}->1; false|{"enum":[0]}->1; 0|{"enum":[false]}->1; true|{"const":1}->1; 1|{"const":true}->1; [true]|{"const":[1]}->1; [1]|{"const":[true]}->1; {"a":true}|{"const":{"a":1}}->1; {"a":1}|{"const":{"a":true}}->1; [true]|{"enum":[[1]]}->1; [1]|{"enum":[[true]]}->1; [[true]]|{"enum":[[[1]]]}->1; {"a":{"b":true}}|{"enum":[{"a":{"b":1}}]}->1; 1.0|{"enum":[true]}->1; true|{"enum":[1.0]}->1; false|{"const":-0.0}->1; [0,1]|{"const":[false,true]}->1. All produce `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`.

rules.rule: true equals true and false equals false (unbool sentinels are stable). {"const":true} with true -> valid.
rules.evidence: true|{"const":true} -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`; false|{"enum":[null,false]} -> 0 errors.

rules.rule: Numbers compare by mathematical value across int/float representations, with ARBITRARY-PRECISION integer semantics. Integer literals must be kept as exact big integers; do NOT coerce to IEEE double. int-vs-float comparison must be exact (compare the float's exact rational value against the big int).
Cross-type never equal: string vs number, string vs boolean, null vs anything else.

Empty enum `{"enum":[]}` is a VALID Draft-7 schema (check_schema does NOT reject it; the draft-07 metaschema declares enum as {type:array, items:true} with no minItems/uniqueItems) and it makes every instance invalid with exactly 1 error.
rules.evidence: 1|{"enum":[]} -> `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`; null|{"enum":[]} -> same; []|{"enum":[]} -> same; true|{"enum":[]} -> same. Exit 0 in all cases, so check_schema did not raise.

rules.rule: Duplicate enum entries are ALSO accepted by check_schema and behave as a plain membership test (no error, no dedup effect).
enum and const are independent keywords: both may be present and each yields its own error, producing 2 separate ErrorTree buckets (keywords "enum" and "const") at the same path.
rules.evidence: 1|{"const":2,"enum":[3]} -> `2 2 2 False False False None None 2 2`; 2|{"enum":[1,3],"const":3} -> 2 2 2 ...; 2|{"enum":[1,2,3],"const":2} -> 0 0 0 True...; 1|{"const":2,"not":{"const":1},"enum":[3]} -> `3 3 3 False False False None None 3 3` (keywords const/not/enum).

rules.rule: ErrorTree (line 1) groups by the pair (absolute instance path, error.validator keyword). Two errors sharing BOTH collapse into one; total = recursive sum over the path tree of the number of distinct keywords at each node. Line 2 is the raw error count.
Collapse is keyed on the FINAL instance path, so errors at different instance paths never collapse even with the same keyword; and sub-tree counts add up.

Keywords that transparently forward child errors to the parent's path — allOf, $ref, if/then/else, dependencies (schema form), patternProperties+properties overlapping the same property, propertyNames — all contribute errors whose keyword is the CHILD keyword and whose path is the descended path, so they can collapse with sibling errors. propertyNames errors keep the PARENT object's path (not the property name), so N bad property names collapse to 1.
anyOf / oneOf / not / contains collapse internally: they emit exactly ONE error at the parent path with their own keyword, never child errors. So they cannot collapse with an inner const/enum error.

Python's json parser is used, so it accepts NaN / Infinity / -Infinity literals in BOTH --a and --b, and it returns the SAME singleton float objects for them. Because equal() short-circuits on object identity, NaN EQUALS NaN under const/enum (contrary to IEEE), and NaN is of type "number".
rules.evidence: NaN|{"const":NaN} -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`; NaN|{"enum":[NaN]} -> 0; [NaN]|{"const":[NaN]} -> 0; --a={"a":NaN} --b={"const":{"a":NaN}} -> 0; --a=NaN --b={"enum":[1,NaN]} -> 0; NaN|{"type":"number"} -> 0; NaN|{"const":1} -> 1 err; 1|{"const":NaN} -> 1 err. Infinity: Infinity|{"const":Infinity} -> 0; Infinity|{"const":1e400} -> 0; 1e400|{"const":Infinity} -> 0; 1e309|{"const":1e309} -> 0; --a=-Infinity --b={"const":-Infinity} -> 0; Infinity|{"const":-1e400} -> 1 err.

rules.rule: Boolean schemas are legal: schema `true` -> 0 errors/valid; schema `false` -> 1 error/invalid. Any other non-object top-level schema (null, string, array) CRASHES before any print.
rules.evidence: 1|true -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`; 1|false -> `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`; 1|[] -> EMPTY exit=1 (AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get' in referencing/jsonschema.py _legacy_dollar_id); 1|null -> EMPTY exit=1 (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable); 1|'"enum"' -> EMPTY exit=1 (AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get').

rules.rule: A non-array `enum` value ALWAYS produces EMPTY/exit=1, but by two different mechanisms: number/null/boolean crash inside iter_errors (TypeError: '<type>' object is not iterable at jsonschema/_keywords.py:270), while string/object survive iter_errors (iterating chars/keys) and then crash in check_schema with SchemaError. Reimplementers can treat all of them uniformly as a hard failure.
rules.evidence: 1|{"enum":1} -> EMPTY exit=1, `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable`; 1|{"enum":null} -> `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable`; 1|{"enum":true} -> `TypeError: 'bool' object is not iterable`; 1|{"enum":"abc"} -> `jsonschema.exceptions.SchemaError: 'abc' is not of type 'array'` / `Failed validating 'type' in metaschema['properties']['enum']: {'type': 'array', 'items': True}`; '"a"'|{"enum":"abc"} -> same SchemaError even though "a" is a member of the chars; 1|{"enum":{"a":1}} -> SchemaError `{'a': 1} is not of type 'array'`.

rules.rule: `const` accepts ANY JSON value with no metaschema restriction (const: null, const: [], const: {} are all fine).
$schema in the schema does not change behavior: the validator is hard-wired to Draft 7 and check_schema always validates against the draft-07 metaschema.
rules.evidence: 1|{"$schema":"http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#","const":2} -> `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`; 1|{"$schema":"http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#","const":2} -> identical output.

rules.rule: Duplicate object keys in the input JSON are resolved last-wins by the parser before comparison.
Strings compare by Unicode code points after JSON unescaping; no normalization.

surprises: NaN == NaN is TRUE here. Python's json decoder returns one shared `float('nan')` singleton for every `NaN` literal, and jsonschema's equal() starts with an `a is b` identity check, so `--a NaN --b '{"const":NaN}'` validates (0 errors). A JS reimplementation using `===`/Object.is-free comparison would report invalid. Same for `[NaN]` vs const `[NaN]` and `{"a":NaN}` vs const `{"a":NaN}`.

JSON input accepts NaN, Infinity, -Infinity and out-of-range literals like 1e400 (-> Infinity). JSON.parse in JS rejects NaN/Infinity outright and silently maps 1e400 to Infinity. Note 1e400 === Infinity here (const:1e400 matches instance Infinity).

Integers are arbitrary precision. 10000000000000000001 !== 10000000000000000002 and 9007199254740993 !== 9007199254740992, but naive JSON.parse in JS collapses all of these to the same double. Must parse integer literals as BigInt (or compare literal text) to reproduce.

int-vs-float comparison is exact, not double-rounded: 1e19 == 10000000000000000000 (valid) but 1e19 != 10000000000000000001 (invalid), and 9007199254740993.0 != 9007199254740993 (the float literal rounds down to ...92). So the float side must be converted to its exact value, not the int side to a float.

Empty enum `[]` and duplicate enum entries are BOTH accepted by Draft-7 check_schema (draft-07 dropped minItems/uniqueItems from the enum metaschema). Many reimplementers assume check_schema rejects them. Empty enum just makes everything invalid with 1 error.

A string enum value (`{"enum":"abc"}`) does NOT crash iter_errors — it iterates characters — but still produces EMPTY output because check_schema raises later. Since all prints happen at the end, you cannot observe the partial success.

The boolean/number guard is recursive through arrays and objects, including inside enum members: `[1]` against `{"enum":[[true]]}` is INVALID. An older jsonschema used `instance not in enums` (Python list `==`), which would call that valid; this build does not.
-0.0 == 0 (valid) but false != -0.0 (the unbool guard beats numeric equality).
A string is never equal to an array of its characters: `"ab"` vs const `["a","b"]` is invalid in both directions.

ErrorTree collapse only requires (path, keyword) to match; the schema location is irrelevant. `{"const":2,"if":{"const":1},"then":{"const":3}}` gives 2 raw errors but treeTotal 1, and `{"dependencies":{"a":{"const":2}},"const":3}` likewise. propertyNames errors are filed under the parent object's path, so 2 bad key names collapse to 1.

argparse artifact: `--a '-Infinity'` fails with exit code 2 ("argument --a: expected one argument") because the value looks like a flag. `--a=-Infinity` works. `--a '-1'` works (looks like a negative number).
